title: "Worked example"
description: >
  A full validation of a treatment-selection model on simulated data, using
  every function in cateval.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.2,
  dpi = 150,
  out.width = "100%",
  dev = "ragg_png"
)
options(pillar.print_min = 6, pillar.width = 90)
```

A treatment-selection model predicts each patient's outcome on every
available treatment and recommends the one with the best prediction. Before
you rely on it, you need two answers:

1. Do patients who receive the recommended treatment do better?
2. Are the predicted differences between treatments the right size?

cateval answers both from data you already hold: the treatment each patient
received, their outcome, and the model's predictions. This example uses
`cateval_example`, a simulated cohort that comes with the package.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(cateval)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## The data

```{r data}
head(cateval_example)
```

Each row is one patient. `treatment` is the treatment they received (`A`, `B`
or `C`), `outcome` is their score after treatment, and `pred_A`, `pred_B` and
`pred_C` hold the model's predicted outcome on each treatment. **Lower is
better** for the outcome and for the predictions; cateval assumes this
throughout.

The simulation has a known answer. Treatment `B` works best for patients with
a high `marker`, and `C` works best for younger patients. The model has learned
this, but it overstates the size of the differences by about 25%. A good
validation should find both things.

Treatment choice depended on age and marker, so the three groups are not
alike at the start:

```{r groups}
cateval_example |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), age = mean(age), marker = mean(marker), baseline = mean(baseline))
```

Comparing raw outcomes between groups would mix the effect of treatment with
these differences. Each analysis below matches or adjusts for them.

### A shared look for the plots

cateval returns tables, and you draw the plots. The plots below share one
small theme and one colour per treatment:

```{r theme}
theme_cateval <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
    axis.text        = element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
    axis.title       = element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
  )

treatment_colours <- c(A = "#2a78d6", B = "#eb6834", C = "#1baf7a")
```

## 1. Recommended treatments

`get_best_drugs()` adds the treatment with the lowest prediction to each row.
`final_var_name` does two jobs: it names the new columns, and cateval removes it
from the prediction column names to get the treatment names (`pred_A` becomes
`A`).

```{r best}
best <- get_best_drugs(
  cateval_example,
  column_names   = c("pred_A", "pred_B", "pred_C"),
  final_var_name = "pred_"
)

table(recommended = best$pred_rank1_drug_name)
```

Each treatment is the top choice for about a third of patients. Often the top
two predictions sit close together, though. With `tolerance`, you get every
treatment whose prediction lies within that distance of the best one, and
`plot_optimal_drugs()` summarises those sets:

```{r near-best, fig.height = 3.6}
near_best <- get_best_drugs(
  cateval_example,
  column_names   = c("pred_A", "pred_B", "pred_C"),
  final_var_name = "pred_",
  tolerance      = 2
)

plot_optimal_drugs(
  near_best$pred_within_2_of_best_drug_name,
  groups   = list("1 treatment" = 1, "2 treatments" = 2, "3 treatments" = 3),
  subtitle = "Within 2 points of each patient's best prediction"
)
```

For `r scales::percent(mean(!grepl(",", near_best$pred_within_2_of_best_drug_name)))`
of patients, one treatment stands clear of the others. The rest have two or
three options that the model rates within 2 points of each other.

## 2. The benefit of following the model

Call a patient **concordant** if they received the treatment the model
recommends for them, and **discordant** if they received a different one.
If the model is useful, concordant patients should do better. A raw comparison
would be unfair, because concordant and discordant patients differ in other
ways. `match_benefit_pairs()` pairs each concordant patient with a similar
discordant patient instead:

- both patients have the same recommended treatment (exact match),
- they received different treatments (always enforced),
- they are close on the matching variables (Mahalanobis distance).

```{r match}
matched <- match_benefit_pairs(
  cateval_example,
  drug_var     = "treatment",
  outcome_var  = "outcome",
  pred_cols    = c("pred_A", "pred_B", "pred_C"),
  matching_var = c("age", "sex", "baseline", "marker"),
  seed         = 1
)

sapply(matched[c("concordant", "discordant", "combined")], nrow)
```

The function matches in both directions. `concordant` holds the pairs built
around concordant patients, `discordant` the pairs built around discordant
patients, and `combined` pools the two without counting a pair twice. The
summaries below use `combined`.

cateval linked each prediction column to its treatment using the column names
and the values in `treatment`. The result is stored with the pairs:

```{r drugs}
matched$drugs
```

If your columns follow a pattern cateval cannot read, pass `drugs = c(...)` in
the same order as `pred_cols`.

### Check the matching

`matched$matchit` holds the MatchIt objects, so you can check balance with
MatchIt's tools. The standardised mean difference (SMD) compares the two sides
of the pairs on each variable. Values near zero after matching mean the paired
patients are alike; a common rule of thumb asks for less than 0.1:

```{r balance}
bal <- summary(matched$matchit$concordant)
round(cbind(
  before = bal$sum.all[, "Std. Mean Diff."],
  after  = bal$sum.matched[, "Std. Mean Diff."]
)[c("age", "baseline", "marker", "sexFemale"), ], 3)
```

`plot(bal)` draws the same numbers as a love plot. It also lists cateval's
internal matching variables (the recommended treatment, which is matched
exactly, and the received treatment, which always differs).

### The headline number

Each pair gives an **observed benefit**: the discordant patient's outcome minus
the concordant patient's. A positive value means the patient on the
recommended treatment did better. The average over all pairs is the benefit of
following the model:

```{r overall}
overall <- benefit_overall(matched$combined)
overall
```

Patients who received the recommended treatment did
`r round(overall$observed, 1)` points better
(95% CI `r round(overall$lower.ci, 1)` to `r round(overall$upper.ci, 1)`)
than similar patients who did not.

### Calibration of the predicted benefit

Each pair also has a **predicted benefit**: the model's expected advantage of
the recommended treatment over the treatment the discordant patient received. `benefit_by_group()` splits the pairs into groups of predicted
benefit and gives the mean observed benefit in each:

```{r by-group}
by_group <- benefit_by_group(matched$combined, cal_groups = 10)
by_group
```

If the model is well calibrated, each group's observed benefit matches its
predicted benefit, so the points fall on the diagonal:

```{r calibration-plot, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5, out.width = "75%", fig.align = "center"}
# the same range on both axes, wide enough for every interval
lims <- range(0, by_group$pred.benefit, by_group$lower.ci, by_group$upper.ci)

ggplot(by_group, aes(x = pred.benefit, y = obs.benefit)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = "#898781") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower.ci, ymax = upper.ci), width = 0, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  coord_equal(xlim = lims, ylim = lims) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted vs observed benefit",
    x = "Predicted benefit (mean per group)",
    y = "Observed benefit (mean, 95% CI)"
  ) +
  theme_cateval
```

The model ranks patients well: groups with a larger predicted benefit gain
more. In the top groups the points sit below the line, so patients there gain
less than the model promises.

Notes on this plot:

- The grey line marks perfect agreement. Equal axis scales (`coord_equal()`)
  keep its slope at 45 degrees, so distances from it are honest.
- `cal_groups` sets the number of groups. More groups show more detail, with
  wider intervals. You can pass several values at once, for example
  `cal_groups = c(5, 10)`; the `n_groups` column then tells them apart.
- A group with fewer than two pairs gets `NA` interval bounds and a warning.

### Calibration in the large and calibration slope

`benefit_citl_slope()` sums up the plot in two numbers, from a regression of
observed on predicted benefit across all pairs:

```{r citl}
cal <- benefit_citl_slope(matched$combined)
cal
```

- **Calibration in the large** (the intercept) is the observed benefit when the
  model predicts none. Near 0 is good; here it is
  `r round(cal$estimate[1], 2)`.
- **Calibration slope** is the rise in observed benefit per unit of
  predicted benefit. A slope of 1 is ideal. Here it is
  `r round(cal$estimate[2], 2)`: patients gain about
  `r round(100 * cal$estimate[2])`% of the predicted benefit. The simulation
  inflated the differences by 25%, so the true slope is 1 / 1.25 = 0.8, and the
  analysis recovers it.

### By treatment

`benefit_by_drug()` repeats the grouped summary for each treatment. Each pair
belongs to the treatment of its index patient (the patient the match was built
around). Pass the full list in `drugs` so every treatment appears in a fixed
order:

```{r by-drug, fig.height = 3.2}
by_drug <- benefit_by_drug(matched$combined, drugs = c("A", "B", "C"), cal_groups = 5)
by_drug <- mutate(by_drug, panel = paste("Treatment", index_drug))

ggplot(by_drug, aes(x = pred.benefit, y = obs.benefit, colour = index_drug)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = "#898781") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower.ci, ymax = upper.ci), width = 0) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = treatment_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-2, 8), ylim = c(-2, 8)) +
  labs(x = "Predicted benefit", y = "Observed benefit") +
  theme_cateval +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
```

The pattern holds for all three treatments, so no single treatment drives the
overstatement.

## 3. Pairwise comparisons: A vs B, A vs C, B vs C

The overall benefit looks at the recommended treatment against everything
else. `pairwise_calibration()` looks at each pair of treatments in turn. For
the pair (A, B):

- the **predicted difference** is `pred_A - pred_B`. Negative values mean the
  model expects A to do better;
- patients are split into groups by that predicted difference;
- one regression of outcome on treatment, across all groups, estimates the
  **observed difference** in each group, A minus B. It is adjusted for the
  variables in `adjustment_var`, with one coefficient per variable shared by
  every group: these only correct for differences between the patients on A
  and on B, so they use all the patients of the pair.

```{r pairwise}
pairwise <- pairwise_calibration(
  cateval_example,
  drug_var        = "treatment",
  drugs           = c("A", "B", "C"),
  prediction_vars = c("pred_A", "pred_B", "pred_C"),
  outcome_var     = "outcome",
  cal_groups      = 5,
  adjustment_var  = c("age", "sex", "baseline", "marker")
)

pairwise |>
  select(drug1, drug2, mean, coef, coef_low, coef_high, n_drug1, n_drug2) |>
  head()
```

`mean` is the mean predicted difference in each group and `coef` the observed
one, with its interval in `coef_low` and `coef_high`. Both use the same scale,
so the diagonal again marks perfect calibration:

```{r pairwise-plot, fig.height = 3.2}
pairwise <- mutate(pairwise, pair = paste(drug1, "vs", drug2))

ggplot(pairwise, aes(x = mean, y = coef)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#e1e0d9") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#e1e0d9") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = "#898781") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = coef_low, ymax = coef_high), width = 0, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  facet_wrap(~ pair) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-7, 7), ylim = c(-7, 7)) +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines")) +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted difference (first minus second)",
    y = "Observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_cateval
```

Bottom-left points are patients for whom the model expects the first treatment
to win; top-right, the second. All three panels rise with the predictions, and
the outer groups again fall short of the diagonal.

The comparison can also match before it estimates. With `matching = TRUE`,
patients predicted to do better on the first treatment are matched to patients
predicted to do better on the second, always across the two treatments. Add
`return_matched = TRUE` to get the matched cohorts back for a balance check.

## 4. Options worth knowing

**Bootstrap intervals.** Every summary gives analytical intervals by default.
The two regressions, `benefit_citl_slope()` and `pairwise_calibration()`, use
HC3 robust standard errors, which allow the spread of the outcome to differ
between patients. Set `bootstrap = TRUE` for percentile bootstrap intervals
that resample the matched pairs:

```{r bootstrap}
benefit_overall(matched$combined, bootstrap = TRUE, n_boot = 500, boot_seed = 1)
```

**Matching settings.** Matching defaults to 1:1 nearest-neighbour Mahalanobis
matching with replacement. You can change it with `replace`, `ratio`,
`caliper` and `method`, or pass any `MatchIt::matchit()` argument through
`match_args`. `match_benefit_pairs()` also takes `match_args_conc` and
`match_args_disc` to set the two directions apart:

```{r options, eval = FALSE}
match_benefit_pairs(
  cateval_example, "treatment", "outcome",
  pred_cols       = c("pred_A", "pred_B", "pred_C"),
  matching_var    = c("age", "sex", "baseline", "marker"),
  match.exact     = "sex",                    # same sex within each pair
  caliper         = c(baseline = 0.25),       # in standard deviations
  match_args_disc = list(replace = FALSE),    # one direction only
  seed            = 1
)
```

**Curved adjustment variables.** In `pairwise_calibration()`, each adjustment
variable enters as a straight line. If a variable's effect on the outcome
bends, give it a curve (a natural spline) with `spline_df`, here with 3
degrees of freedom:

```{r splines}
curved <- pairwise_calibration(
  cateval_example,
  drug_var        = "treatment",
  drugs           = c("A", "B", "C"),
  prediction_vars = c("pred_A", "pred_B", "pred_C"),
  outcome_var     = "outcome",
  cal_groups      = 5,
  adjustment_var  = c("age", "sex", "baseline", "marker"),
  spline_df       = c(baseline = 3)   # only baseline as a curve
)

# largest change in an observed difference
max(abs(curved$coef - pairwise$coef))
```

The simulation gave every variable a straight-line effect, so the curve
changes little against intervals of about ±1. `spline_df = 3` makes every
continuous adjustment variable a curve.

**Read the intervals with care.** With replacement (the default), one control
patient can appear in several pairs. Neither interval accounts for that, so
both run a little narrow when controls are reused often. `replace = FALSE`
removes the issue at the cost of fewer, less close matches.

**Your own data.** Column and treatment names can be anything: `drug_var`,
`outcome_var` and the prediction columns are all arguments. The outcome must
be continuous, with lower values better. If higher is better for your outcome,
multiply the outcome and the predictions by -1 first.

## Functions used

| Step | Function | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| Recommended treatment | `get_best_drugs()` | the best (or near-best) treatment per patient |
| | `plot_optimal_drugs()` | a chart of near-best treatment sets |
| Overall benefit | `match_benefit_pairs()` | matched concordant/discordant pairs |
| | `benefit_overall()` | mean benefit of following the model |
| | `benefit_by_group()` | observed vs predicted benefit by group |
| | `benefit_citl_slope()` | calibration in the large and slope |
| | `benefit_by_drug()` | the grouped summary for each treatment |
| Pairwise effects | `pairwise_calibration()` | observed vs predicted difference for every pair |
| | `pairwise_calibration_pair()` | the same for one pair |
